title: The Canonical Derandomizer: The Derandomization Paradigm, Inverted

reading.text: Self-contained lesson. Optional background: Goldreich's Primer, Ch. 3.1 (canonical derandomizers).

body:
## Why derandomization re-opens the definition

Chapter 2 built **general-purpose pseudorandom generators**: deterministic polynomial-time algorithms whose output is indistinguishable from uniform by *any* efficient observer, so one generator's output may substitute for coin tosses in every efficient application. The archetypal use is derandomization: shrink an algorithm's randomness with a generator, then enumerate all seeds. Theorem 2.16 (Module 5) pushed that route as far as it goes there — a non-uniformly strong PRG (Definition 2.15) places BPP in $\bigcap_{\varepsilon > 0} \mathrm{Dtime}(2^{n^\varepsilon})$ — but not all the way to $\mathrm{BPP} = \mathrm{P}$. The reason is the *stretch*: a polynomial-time generator has polynomial stretch, so feeding $t(n)$ coins needs seeds of length $t(n)^{\Omega(1)}$, and enumeration costs $2^{t(n)^{\Omega(1)}}$.

Chapter 3 of the Primer opens by questioning the premise. **When derandomization proceeds by seed enumeration, the simulation pays a factor $2^k$ anyway — one run of the algorithm per seed — so there is no point in insisting the generator run in time polynomial in $k$: an exponential (in $k$) running time is absorbed by an overhead that is exponential regardless.** And once the generator may run longer than the algorithm it feeds, it only needs to fool distinguishers that take *fewer* steps than itself. Both relaxations are exactly what the application needs: $G$'s output is consumed by one specific algorithm $A$, and the only question is whether $A$'s behavior changes when its coin tosses $U_{\ell(k)}$ are replaced by $G(U_k)$.

Every pseudorandom generator is an instance of one general paradigm, fixed by **three fundamental aspects** — the *stretch*, the *class of distinguishers*, and the *resources of the generator itself*. General-purpose generators set the default (polynomial-time $G$, polynomial stretch, uniform PPT distinguishers); derandomization re-sets all three:

| Fundamental aspect | General-purpose PRG (Ch. 2, Def. 2.1) | Canonical derandomizer (Def. 3.1) |
|---|---|---|
| **Stretch** (output vs. seed length) | $\ell(k) > k$, in practice $\ell(k) = \mathrm{poly}(k)$; Sec. 2.4 amplification raises any stretch to any desired polynomial | $\ell(k)$ as large as possible — the target is **exponential stretch $\ell(k) = 2^{\Omega(k)}$**, at the ceiling $O(2^k)$ (super-exponential is impossible, Theorem 3.3) |
| **Complexity of the generator vs. the distinguisher** | generator runs in $\mathrm{poly}(k)$; the distinguisher may be *stronger* — any uniform PPT machine, i.e., time $p(t_G(k))$ for every polynomial $p$ | generator runs in $\mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k))$, which may exceed the circuits it fools: $t_G(k) > \ell(k)^2$, even $t_G(k) > 2^k$, is allowed |
| **Uniformity of the distinguisher class; form of the gap** | uniform PPT algorithm (with internal coins); gap negligible, $< 1/p(k)$ for every polynomial $p$; non-uniform variant (Def. 2.15): poly-size circuits, still negligible gap | non-uniform circuit family $\{D_k\}$, each of size $\ell(k)^2$; gap the absolute constant $1/6$; a per-length guarantee "in the strong sense" |
| **Role of the output** | universal: interchangeable with uniform bits in every efficient application | purpose-built: replace only the coin tosses of one $\mathrm{BPtime}(t)$ algorithm — fool the size-$\ell(k)^2$ circuits $C_x = A(x, \cdot)$ that model it |

Rows 2 and 3 are the **paradigm inversion**: in Chapter 2 the generator is the fast party and the distinguishers may be stronger than it; in the derandomization setting the generator may be exponentially slower than the circuits it fools, and it need only fool those.

## The stage: BPtime(t) and the emulation circuits that must be fooled

@def:bp-time

Now fix $A \in \mathrm{BPtime}(t)$ and write $A(x, r)$ for the output of $A$ on input $x$ with coin tosses $r \in \{0,1\}^{t(|x|)}$. Hard-wiring $x$ into $A$ gives the **emulation circuit**

$$C_x(r) \;=\; A(x, r)$$

of input length $t(n)$ and size at most $t(n)^2$ (quadratic in its input length, by standard Turing-machine-to-circuit emulation; padding lets size equal input length). Eq. (3.1) is really about these: for fixed $x$, "does replacing $U_{t(n)}$ by $G(U_k)$ change $A$'s decision on $x$?" is exactly "does $C_x$ behave the same on the two distributions?"

If the replacement coins are $G(s)$ for $s \in \{0,1\}^k$, we need $\ell(k) \ge t(n)$: take $k = \ell^{-1}(t(n))$, the smallest integer with $\ell(k) \ge t(n)$ (feeding $A$ the $t(n)$-bit prefix of $G(s)$ when the inequality is strict, as in Construction 2.2). After padding $C_x$'s input to $\ell(k)$ bits, $C_x$ has size at most $t(n)^2 \le \ell(k)^2$. **The derandomizer must fool precisely the circuits $\{C_x\}$ — one per input, each of size at most $\ell(k)^2$ — and Definition 3.1 demands exactly that, uniformly over all circuits of that size.**

## Definition 3.1: a generator allowed to be slower than its distinguishers

@def:canonical

Reading the definition, each clause earns its place:

- **Deterministic, monotone stretch $\ell$.** On $k$-bit seeds $G$ outputs exactly $\ell(k)$ bits, with $\ell: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ monotonically increasing. Monotonicity lets a derandomizer *find* $k = \ell^{-1}(t(n))$ by invoking $G(1^i)$ until output length $\ell(i)$ reaches $t(n)$.
- **Time $\mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k))$, not $\mathrm{poly}(k)$.** The simulation pays $2^k$ regardless, so exponential time is affordable. The factor $\ell(k)$ only keeps the door open for super-exponential stretch in principle; Eq. (3.1) slams it shut (Theorem 3.3), so effectively $\mathrm{poly}(2^k)$.
- **Fools every circuit of size $\ell(k)^2$.** A non-uniform family $\{D_k\}$: no constructibility or cross-length consistency required, one fixed budget per length. The class excludes machines that can run the generator — evaluating $G$ costs $\gg \ell(k)^2$ — the asymmetry that powers the next lesson.
- **Gap $< 1/6$: an absolute constant, "in the strong sense".** With error $1/3$, acceptance on yes-instances is $\ge 2/3$; since $2/3 - 1/6 = 1/2$, the gap pushes acceptance strictly across the majority threshold (symmetrically for no-instances). Even a constant advantage of $1/6$ is too much.
- **No negligible functions.** In Chapter 2 gaps must be negligible because a PPT distinguisher can amplify a constant advantage by repetition. Here the procedure enumerates *all* $2^k$ seeds, so only the *mean* of the votes matters — no sampling error to concentrate away — and repetition would burst the fixed size class $\ell(k)^2$. A constant gap below $1/2$ is the right currency — and all that is achievable.

## Proposition 3.2: stretch is a resource, and derandomization spends it

@thm:prop32

The formula is the accounting of the module's first half: **deterministic time is exponential in the seed length $k = \ell^{-1}(t(n))$ that suffices to feed $t(n)$ coins, and polynomial in everything else.** Each of the $2^k$ seeds costs one simulation of $A$ on $G(s)$ — $\mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k)) + t(n)$, which is $\le \mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k))$ since $\ell(k) \ge t(n)$ — so the total is $\mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k)) = \mathrm{poly}(2^{\ell^{-1}(t(n))} \cdot t(n))$. Two facts deserve emphasis:

- **The derandomized machine is uniform.** $G$ is fixed and seed enumeration is a plain loop; no advice is needed, though the correctness argument quantifies over the non-uniform circuits $C_x$ one input at a time. Non-uniformity lives in the *analysis*, not the algorithm.
- **The derandomized procedure is error-free.** Eq. (3.1) forces strictly more than half of the seeds to vote correctly on every input, so the deterministic majority is right on all sufficiently long inputs: substitution preserves the *sign* of $\Pr[A(x, U) = 1] - 1/2$, and the majority uses nothing else.

Sanity check at the low end: even a (hypothetical) minimal-stretch derandomizer, $\ell(k) = k+1$, would give $T(n) \approx \mathrm{poly}(2^{t(n)})$ — no better than exhaustive enumeration. **Stretch is the entire currency of derandomization.**

## Theorem 3.3: exponential stretch is exactly the prize

@thm:thm33

Why is $2^{\Omega(k)}$ *exactly* the prize — simultaneously sufficient and essentially maximal?

- **Sufficiency — enumeration becomes polynomial.** With $\ell(k) = 2^{\Omega(k)}$, a polynomial number $t(n)$ of coins is fed from a seed of length $O(\log t(n)) = O(\log n)$; enumerating all $2^k$ seeds costs $2^{O(\log n)} = \mathrm{poly}(n)$, so Proposition 3.2 gives $\mathrm{BPtime}(t) \subseteq \mathrm{Dtime}(\mathrm{poly}(t(n)))$ for every polynomial $t$ — and $\mathrm{BPP} = \bigcup_c \mathrm{BPtime}(n^c)$ collapses into $\mathrm{P}$.
- **Necessity — the boundary is exact.** With merely polynomial stretch, $\ell(k) = k^a$, feeding $t(n) = n^c$ coins needs a seed of length $n^{c/a}$; enumeration then costs $2^{n^{c/a}}$ — exponential. Seed enumeration is polynomial iff seeds of length $O(\log t(n))$ suffice iff $\ell(k) = 2^{\Omega(k)}$.
- **Ceiling — nothing larger can exist.** $\ell(k) = \omega(2^k)$ violates Eq. (3.1): a circuit hard-wiring the whole range separates $G(U_k)$ from $U_{\ell(k)}$ with gap near $1$, in size $O(2^k \cdot \ell(k)) < \ell(k)^2$ (proof in the theorem's field). Exponential stretch is thus the strongest hypothesis of this form that can hold.

This is why Theorem 2.16 (Module 5) and Theorem 3.3 differ despite the same proof architecture: the former pays $2^{n^\varepsilon}$ for enumerating seeds of a polynomial-stretch generator; the latter pays $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.

## Statistically far, yet computationally indistinguishable

Confront the paradox head-on. If $\ell(k) \gg k$, then $G(U_k)$ is supported on at most $2^k$ points of $\{0,1\}^{\ell(k)}$, while $U_{\ell(k)}$ spreads mass over $2^{\ell(k)}$ points; the variation distance is at least $1 - 2^{k-\ell(k)}$ (mass overlap at most $2^k \cdot 2^{-\ell(k)}$) — for exponential stretch, $1 - 2^{-(2^{\Omega(k)}-k)}$, i.e. statistically *maximally* far, and any unlimited statistical test separates them instantly. Yet Definition 3.1 demands that circuits of size $\ell(k)^2$ cannot tell them apart. The resolution is the "behavioristic" stance of the paradigm (Primer, §2.8): (pseudo)randomness is a property of the *observer*. A distribution ontologically very different from uniform — an exponentially sparse support — looks uniform to every observer too weak to exploit the difference, and the natural exploit (enumerate seeds, check range membership) costs $2^k \cdot t_G(k)$, far beyond the $\ell(k)^2$ budget of the observers that matter. No contradiction arises: Definition 3.1 never promised protection against powerful tests, only against the $C_x$'s — all derandomization needs (the deterministic simulator may know everything about $G$: it runs $G$).

## Who exactly must be fooled: circuit families, not uniform machines

Consider the *uniform* algorithm $E$ that, on input $y$, enumerates all $2^k$ seeds, evaluates $G$ on each, and accepts iff $y$ matches an output. Then $\Pr[E(G(U_k)) = 1] = 1$ but $\Pr[E(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1] = 2^{k - \ell(k)}$: a perfect statistical test. Why does this not refute Definition 3.1? Because $E$ is not a circuit of size $\ell(k)^2$: it runs in time $2^k \cdot t_G(k) \ge 2^k \cdot \ell(k) > \ell(k)^2$ whenever $\ell(k) < 2^k$ — and $\ell(k) \ge 2^k$ is impossible anyway. Uniform machines of time $\tau$ give circuits of size roughly $\tau$, so size-$\ell(k)^2$ security corresponds to uniform time about $\ell(k)$; the enumerator needs uniform time about $2^k$ — exponentially beyond the budget. The *uniform vs. circuit* choice genuinely changes the answer:

- If Definition 3.1 quantified over uniform machines running in time $\mathrm{poly}(2^k)$ — even $2^{1.1k}$ — **no** exponential-stretch generator could exist: the enumerator refutes each. Security against such machines is impossible and, crucially, unnecessary.
- In Chapter 2 the mirror image holds: $t_G(k) = \mathrm{poly}(k)$, and indistinguishability is required against uniform PPT machines — time $p(t_G(k))$ for *every* polynomial $p$; the distinguisher may be polynomially stronger than the generator, whereas a canonical derandomizer is broken by any machine allowed a polynomial factor over its exponential runtime.
- The derandomized conclusions (Proposition 3.2, Theorem 3.3) are nonetheless uniform: the size-$\ell(k)^2$ guarantee is invoked only on the $C_x$'s a hypothetical bad input would produce, and the procedure never constructs them — a non-uniform *hypothesis* yields a uniform *conclusion*.
- **Preview of the next lesson.** Because the fooled circuits are *smaller* than the generator, pseudorandomness can survive even a distinguisher handed the seed itself: a seed-aware circuit of size $\ell(k)^2$ cannot run $G$ on it, nor try all $2^k$ seeds. For Chapter 2 generators this is impossible — a seed-aware PPT distinguisher just evaluates the polynomial-time $G$.

## Why the Chapter 2 toolbox dies in this regime

The inversion is not free: techniques built for a fast generator facing weaker-or-equal distinguishers break when the generator is the slower party.

- **Re-seeding / stretch amplification (Section 2.4) is unusable.** Amplification proofs are reductions: to prove the amplified generator secure, one converts a distinguisher of it into a distinguisher of the *base* generator by a hybrid argument whose intermediate distributions *simulate the base generator internally*. In Chapter 2 this is sound — the generator is polynomial-time and the distinguishers PPT, so the reduction's output stays efficient. In the canonical regime the base generator runs in time $2^{\Omega(k)} > \ell(k)^2$: any reduction that evaluates it produces a "distinguisher" far larger than the size budget under which the derandomizer must operate, so the reduction cannot live inside the adversary class of Definition 3.1. There is also nothing to amplify *toward*: re-seeding compounds polynomial stretch into polynomial stretch, while the goal is the exponential ceiling — which must be built **in one shot**, as the next lesson does by drawing all $\ell(k)$ output bits from a single seed through many overlapping windows, not by iteration.
- **The raw material changes.** Chapter 2 converted one-wayness into pseudorandomness; exponential-stretch derandomizers cannot be analyzed that way (the reductions would have to invert or evaluate the generator inside tiny circuits). The next lesson instead consumes Boolean predicates computable in exponential time yet *inapproximable* by small circuits; as with general-purpose PRGs, such hardness is essentially *necessary* (Primer, end of §3.2).

## Why this matters

- **The paradigm inversion is the module's engine.** Derandomization lets the generator run longer than the circuits it fools — seed enumeration already costs $2^k$, and only the emulation circuits $C_x$ of size $\le \ell(k)^2$ need fooling. The Nisan–Wigderson construction and its analysis rest entirely on this relaxation.
- **Proposition 3.2 is the stretch-to-time conversion machine; Theorem 3.3 locates the break-even point.** Stretch $2^{\Omega(k)}$ is simultaneously necessary for polynomial-time derandomization of all of BPP and the largest stretch that can exist — the prize is the ceiling. Weaker hardness assumptions still derandomize BPP, only slower (Theorem 3.6, next lesson).
- **Constant gaps plus full enumeration are a feature.** The simulation runs on every seed and majority-votes, so only the sign of the acceptance mean must be preserved — hence the constant $1/6$, no negligible functions, and exact (error-free) derandomization rather than bounded-error simulation.
- **Randomness is observer-relative.** $G(U_k)$ is statistically almost maximally far from uniform, yet computationally indistinguishable from it to the observers that matter. Derandomization is the art of choosing the right observers — and of letting the generator be slow enough to fool them.

defs.name: BPtime(t): bounded-error probabilistic time
defs.statement:
Fixing a model of computation, $\mathrm{BPtime}(t)$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by a randomized algorithm $A$ of time complexity $t$ that has **two-sided error $1/3$**: on inputs of length $n$, $A$ runs in time at most $t(n)$ (hence tosses at most $t(n)$ coins), and for every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$,

$$x \in S \;\Rightarrow\; \Pr_{r \leftarrow U_{t(n)}}[A(x, r) = 1] \;\ge\; \frac{2}{3}, \qquad\qquad x \notin S \;\Rightarrow\; \Pr_{r \leftarrow U_{t(n)}}[A(x, r) = 1] \;\le\; \frac{1}{3}$$

and $\mathrm{BPP} = \bigcup_{c \ge 1} \mathrm{BPtime}(n^c + c)$. The error bound $1/3$ is a convention (any constant below $1/2$ would give the same class, since error can be amplified by repetition), and the threshold gap $1/6$ of Eq. (3.1) is calibrated to it: if $\Pr[D_k(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1] \ge 2/3$ then $\Pr[D_k(G(U_k)) = 1] > 1/2$, and dually $\le 1/3$ gives $< 1/2$ — exactly the margin a majority vote over seeds requires.
defs.intuition: BPtime(t) is the class the module wants to derandomize: bounded-error (two-sided error 1/3), time- and randomness-complexity t. The pairing 'error 1/3, gap 1/6' is calibrated so that a yes-instance's acceptance probability 2/3 survives any allowed substitution as acceptance strictly above 1/2 — the knife's edge on which majority voting turns.

defs.name: Definition 3.1 (canonical derandomizer of stretch $\ell$)
defs.statement:
Let $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a monotonically increasing function. A **canonical derandomizer of stretch $\ell$** is a deterministic algorithm $G$ that satisfies the following two conditions:

1. **Complexity.** On input a $k$-bit long seed, $G$ makes at most $\mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k))$ steps and outputs a string of length $\ell(k)$.
2. **Pseudorandomness (Eq. (3.1)).** For every circuit $D_k$ of size $\ell(k)^2$ it holds that

$$\left|\Pr[D_k(G(U_k)) = 1] - \Pr[D_k(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1]\right| \;<\; \frac{1}{6}$$

The circuit $D_k$ represents a potential distinguisher, which is given an $\ell(k)$-bit long string (sampled either from $G(U_k)$ or from $U_{\ell(k)}$); the bound is required to hold in the **strong sense** — even a constant distinguishing gap of $1/6$ is ruled out.
defs.intuition: The definition re-balances the three fundamental aspects for the derandomization application: the generator may be exponentially slower than the objects it fools (the simulation pays 2^k for seed enumeration anyway, and the only circuits that must be fooled are the emulation circuits C_x of size at most ℓ(k)²); the distinguishers are demoted from 'every efficient machine' to 'every circuit of size ℓ(k)²' (non-uniform, fixed budget per length); and the gap is the constant 1/6, calibrated to two-sided error 1/3 so that majority voting over all seeds goes through. In particular t_G(k) > ℓ(k)² — even t_G(k) > 2^k — is allowed: the generator may be larger than every machine it fools.

theorems.name: Proposition 3.2 (derandomizing BPtime(t) with a canonical derandomizer)
theorems.statement:
Let $\ell, t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be monotonically increasing functions, and let $\ell^{-1}(t(n))$ denote the smallest integer $k$ such that $\ell(k) \ge t(n)$. If there exists a canonical derandomizer of stretch $\ell$, then for every time-constructible $t$ it holds that

$$\mathrm{BPtime}(t) \;\subseteq\; \mathrm{Dtime}(T), \qquad\qquad T(n) = \mathrm{poly}\left(2^{\ell^{-1}(t(n))} \cdot t(n)\right)$$

where the polynomial is determined by the generator's complexity bound.
theorems.intuition: The deterministic simulation enumerates all 2^k seeds, k = ℓ^{-1}(t(n)), runs A on G(s) for each, and outputs the majority. Correctness: for each input x the emulation circuit C_x(r) = A(x, r) has size ≤ t(n)² ≤ ℓ(k)², so Eq. (3.1) keeps the vote mean strictly above 1/2 on yes-instances and strictly below 1/2 on no-instances. Time: 2^k simulations each costing poly(2^k·ℓ(k)), which is poly(2^k·ℓ(k)) in total — dominated by the 2^k seed enumeration. Stretch is the currency: the faster ℓ grows, the shorter the seed that feeds t(n) coins, the cheaper the enumeration.
theorems.proof:
Sketch (mimicking the proof of Theorem 2.16 via Construction 2.2). Given $A \in \mathrm{BPtime}(t)$ and an input $x$ of length $n$:

- **Find the seed length.** Invoke $G(1^i)$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots$ until the output length $\ell(i)$ first reaches $t(n)$; since $\ell$ is monotonically increasing and $G$ is a fixed algorithm whose output length on $i$-bit seeds is $\ell(i)$, the first such $i$ is $k = \ell^{-1}(t(n))$. If $\ell(k) > t(n)$, use the $t(n)$-bit prefix of $G(s)$ (as in Construction 2.2).
- **Vote.** Output the majority of the $2^k$ values $A(x, G(s))$ over $s \in \{0,1\}^k$.
- **Correctness.** Hard-wire $x$ into $A$: the circuit $C_x(r) = A(x, r)$ has input length $t(n)$ and size at most $t(n)^2$ (standard Turing-machine-to-circuit emulation); pad its input to $\ell(k)$ bits, obtaining a circuit of size at most $t(n)^2 \le \ell(k)^2$. If $x$ is a yes-instance then $\Pr[C_x(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1] \ge 2/3$, and Eq. (3.1) with $D_k = C_x$ yields $\Pr_s[C_x(G(U_k)) = 1] > 2/3 - 1/6 = 1/2$: strictly more than half of the seeds vote 1, so the majority is 1 — correct. The no-instance case is symmetric: $\Pr[C_x(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1] \le 1/3$ forces $\Pr_s[C_x(G(U_k)) = 1] < 1/2$, so the majority is 0.
- **Time.** Each of the $2^k$ invocations costs $t(n) + \mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k)) \le \mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k))$ (using $\ell(k) \ge t(n)$), for a total of $\mathrm{poly}(2^k \cdot \ell(k)) = \mathrm{poly}(2^{\ell^{-1}(t(n))} \cdot t(n))$. No advice is used anywhere; the procedure is uniform and error-free on all sufficiently long inputs. $\square$

theorems.name: Theorem 3.3 (exponential stretch derandomizes BPP completely)
theorems.statement: If there exists a canonical derandomizer of stretch $\ell(k) = 2^{\Omega(k)}$, then $\mathrm{BPP} = \mathrm{P}$.
theorems.intuition: Exponential stretch is exactly the prize, from both directions at once. Sufficiency: ℓ(k) = 2^{Ω(k)} means ℓ^{-1}(t(n)) = O(log t(n)): a polynomial number t(n) of coins is fed by seeds of length O(log n), so enumerating all 2^k seeds costs poly(n) and Proposition 3.2 yields BPtime(t) ⊆ Dtime(poly(t(n))) — polynomial time for every polynomial t, hence BPP = P. The boundary is exact: with merely polynomial stretch ℓ(k) = k^a the same proposition gives T(n) = poly(2^{n^{c/a}}), exponential. And the stretch cannot be pushed higher: ℓ(k) = ω(2^k) is impossible, since a circuit that hard-wires the generator's whole range — size O(2^k·ℓ(k)) < ℓ(k)² — separates G(U_k) from U_ℓ(k) with gap close to 1. So 2^{Ω(k)} is simultaneously the condition that collapses seed enumeration to polynomial time and the largest stretch a canonical derandomizer can have: the prize is the ceiling.
theorems.proof:
Let $G$ be a canonical derandomizer of stretch $\ell(k) = 2^{\Omega(k)}$: there exist constants $c > 0$ and $k_0$ such that $\ell(k) \ge 2^{ck}$ for all $k \ge k_0$. For every time-constructible polynomial $t$ and all sufficiently large $n$,

$$\ell^{-1}(t(n)) \;\le\; \max\left(k_0,\; \frac{\log_2 t(n)}{c}\right) = O(\log t(n)) = O(\log n)$$

since $t(n) = n^{O(1)}$. Proposition 3.2 gives $\mathrm{BPtime}(t) \subseteq \mathrm{Dtime}(T)$ with

$$T(n) = \mathrm{poly}\left(2^{\ell^{-1}(t(n))} \cdot t(n)\right) = \mathrm{poly}\left(2^{O(\log n)} \cdot t(n)\right) = \mathrm{poly}(t(n))$$

a polynomial. Taking $t$ over all polynomials and using $\mathrm{BPP} = \bigcup_{c \ge 1} \mathrm{BPtime}(n^c + c)$, we get $\mathrm{BPP} \subseteq \bigcup_c \mathrm{Dtime}(\mathrm{poly}(n^c)) = \mathrm{P}$; the reverse inclusion is trivial (a deterministic algorithm is a randomized one that ignores its coins). Hence $\mathrm{BPP} = \mathrm{P}$. $\square$

Why the stretch assumption sits exactly at the boundary:

- **Below the boundary.** With only polynomial stretch, say $\ell(k) = k^a$, one has $\ell^{-1}(t(n)) = t(n)^{1/a} = n^{c/a}$ for $t(n) = n^c$, and $T(n) = \mathrm{poly}(2^{n^{c/a}})$ — exponential; Proposition 3.2 cannot derandomize BPP in polynomial time from such a generator.
- **Above the boundary there is nothing.** Super-exponential stretch $\ell(k) = \omega(2^k)$ is impossible for any canonical derandomizer. Let $D_k$ be the circuit that hard-wires the table of all $2^k$ outputs $G(s)$ (size $O(2^k \cdot \ell(k))$) and accepts an input iff it matches a table entry. Then $\Pr[D_k(G(U_k)) = 1] = 1$ while $\Pr[D_k(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1] = 2^k \cdot 2^{-\ell(k)} = 2^{k - \ell(k)} \le 1/16$ for all large $k$ (as $\ell(k) = \omega(2^k)$), a gap exceeding $15/16 > 1/6$; and the circuit's size $O(2^k \cdot \ell(k)) < \ell(k)^2$ precisely when $\ell(k) = \omega(2^k)$ — violating Eq. (3.1). Hence every canonical derandomizer has $\ell(k) = O(2^k)$, and exponential stretch $2^{\Omega(k)}$ is the strongest hypothesis of this form that can possibly hold. $\square$

checkpoints.question: Relative to Chapter 2's general-purpose pseudorandom generators, what exactly does the derandomization setting invert, and which of the following states the inversion correctly?

options.text: The allowed complexity asymmetry. A canonical derandomizer may run in time poly(2^k·ℓ(k)) — exponential in its seed length and larger than the size ℓ(k)² of the circuits it fools, even larger than 2^k — because the derandomizing simulation enumerates all 2^k seeds and pays that exponential overhead regardless; and it only needs to fool the size-ℓ(k)² circuits that model 'the randomized algorithm A with input x hard-wired' (the emulation circuits C_x), not all uniform PPT machines. In Chapter 2, by contrast, the generator is polynomial-time while the distinguishers may be polynomially more powerful than it.
The stretch: canonical derandomizers must output exponentially more bits than the seed contains, whereas general-purpose generators may only shrink the seed (ℓ(k) < k).

The uniformity: a canonical derandomizer is itself a non-uniform algorithm (a different circuit per seed length), whereas a general-purpose generator is uniform; the classes of distinguishers are unchanged.
The error model: canonical derandomizers are permitted a one-sided error of 1/6 in their output, whereas general-purpose generators must be correct on every output bit with probability 1.

checkpoints.explanation: The inversion is in the resource asymmetry (row 2 of the three-aspect comparison): in Chapter 2 the generator is the fast party (poly(k)) and the distinguishers may be stronger (uniform PPT, i.e., time p(t_G(k)) for any polynomial p); in Definition 3.1 the generator may be the slow party (poly(2^k·ℓ(k)), possibly exceeding ℓ(k)² and even 2^k) because the simulation pays 2^k for seed enumeration anyway. The stretch target also changes (poly → exponential), and the distinguisher class shrinks from all uniform PPT machines to circuits of size ℓ(k)² with a constant 1/6 gap. The wrong options misstate the facts: both kinds of generator stretch (ℓ(k) > k); the generator itself is a deterministic uniform algorithm in both settings (what changes is that the adversaries form a non-uniform family of bounded-size circuits); and Eq. (3.1) is a distinguishing-gap requirement on the generator — the derandomized procedure of Proposition 3.2 is deterministic and error-free.

checkpoints.question: Why is the distinguishing gap in Eq. (3.1) the absolute constant 1/6 rather than a negligible function, and why does the majority-vote derandomization of Proposition 3.2 go through with such a coarse gap?

options.text: BPtime(t) allows two-sided error 1/3, so on a yes-instance the acceptance probability of the emulation circuit satisfies Pr[C_x(U_ℓ(k))=1] ≥ 2/3, and Eq. (3.1) forces Pr_s[C_x(G(U_k))=1] > 2/3 − 1/6 = 1/2 (symmetrically, ≤ 1/3 gives < 1/2 on no-instances). The deterministic simulation evaluates A(x, G(s)) for every seed s and takes a majority — an exact enumeration, not a sample — so only the sign of the vote mean matters and no concentration bound is needed; a constant gap strictly below 1/2 suffices. The value 1/6 is exactly the slack between the acceptance threshold 2/3 and the majority threshold 1/2, and both inequalities are strict.
The gap must be smaller than 1/(6·2^k), so that a union bound over the 2^k votes keeps the probability that the majority errs below 1/3; 1/6 is a per-seed error budget.
1/6 is the standard Chernoff-bound constant: it guarantees that the majority over 2^k pseudorandom samples is correct with probability at least 1 − 2^{−k}.

The gap is chosen small enough that any distinguisher with advantage ≥ 1/6 can be amplified by repetition into a negligible advantage, matching Chapter 2's convention that gaps must vanish faster than any polynomial.

checkpoints.explanation: Because the derandomization enumerates all 2^k seeds, the vote count is exact and deterministic: the fraction of seeds voting 1 is precisely Pr_s[A(x, G(s)) = 1], and Eq. (3.1) applied to D_k = C_x pushes that fraction strictly across 1/2 exactly when the input is a yes-instance (2/3 − 1/6 = 1/2 is the knife's edge, with strict inequalities on both sides). No Chernoff bound is needed (there is no sampling), no union bound over seeds is needed (every seed is used), and no repetition amplification is needed (or possible: repeating a test would multiply circuit size beyond ℓ(k)², leaving the quantified class). A negligible gap would be both unattainable — G(U_k) is statistically far from U_ℓ(k) at exponential stretch — and unnecessary.

checkpoints.question: A uniform algorithm E that enumerates all 2^k seeds, evaluates G on each, and checks whether its input matches one of the outputs distinguishes G(U_k) from U_ℓ(k) perfectly (Pr[E(G(U_k))=1] = 1 versus Pr[E(U_ℓ(k))=1] = 2^{k−ℓ(k)}). Why does this not refute Definition 3.1, and what does the distinction between uniform machines and circuit families buy here?

options.text: E is not among the adversaries Definition 3.1 quantifies over: it runs in time 2^k·t_G(k) ≥ 2^k·ℓ(k) > ℓ(k)² (for every legitimate stretch ℓ(k) < 2^k, and ℓ(k) ≥ 2^k is impossible anyway), so E is not a circuit of size ℓ(k)² — the only objects Eq. (3.1) must fool. Uniform machines of time τ are emulated by circuits of size roughly τ, so size-ℓ(k)² security corresponds to uniform time about ℓ(k); the enumerator lives at uniform time about 2^k, exponentially beyond the budget. This is exactly as strong as the application needs: the circuits that must be fooled are the emulation circuits C_x of size ≤ t(n)² ≤ ℓ(k)², and the derandomized simulator may itself know G (it runs G) — there is no adversary left in the final deterministic algorithm.
It does refute Definition 3.1 — which is why canonical derandomizers can only exist with polynomial stretch, and Theorem 3.3 is vacuous.
The enumerator fails because G is a randomized algorithm whose output cannot be reproduced deterministically even when the seed is known.
Definition 3.1 protects the generator only against distinguishers that do not know the seed length k; the enumerator knows k, so it falls outside the model.

checkpoints.explanation: Definition 3.1's quantifier is over circuits of size ℓ(k)² — a fixed, non-uniform size budget per length — and the enumerator's complexity 2^k·t_G(k) exceeds that budget exponentially (uniform τ-time machines give circuits of size ≈ τ, so the enumerator corresponds to a circuit far larger than ℓ(k)²). The right option captures the design logic: the class of circuits that must be fooled is exactly the class containing the C_x's, and derandomization needs nothing more; security against poly(2^k)-time uniform machines is impossible (the enumerator) and unnecessary (the final algorithm is deterministic and runs the generator itself). The wrong options misread the model: the enumerator is a legitimate attack outside the size bound, not an internal contradiction; G is deterministic; and the seed length k is known to every distinguisher in the definition.

exercises.prompt: Contrast a general-purpose pseudorandom generator (Definition 2.1, plus its non-uniformly strong variant Definition 2.15) with a canonical derandomizer (Definition 3.1) along the three fundamental aspects of the general paradigm: (i) stretch (seed length vs. output length); (ii) the complexity of the generator relative to the complexity of the distinguisher; (iii) the uniformity of the distinguisher class and the quantitative form of the indistinguishability requirement. Produce a comparison table, and for each aspect add one sentence explaining why the derandomization setting's choice is exactly what the application needs (think: the 2^k seed-enumeration overhead; the emulation circuits C_x = A(x, ·) of size ≤ t(n)²; majority voting over all seeds). Finally, explain in two sentences why Theorem 2.16 (Module 5) yields only BPP ⊆ Dtime(2^{n^ε}) for every ε > 0, whereas Theorem 3.3 yields BPP = P.
exercises.hint: Structure your answer by the three aspects. (i) Compare ℓ(k) = poly(k), amplifiable to any polynomial via Section 2.4, with ℓ(k) = 2^{Ω(k)} at the ceiling O(2^k). (ii) Compare 'generator poly(k), distinguisher any uniform PPT machine (time p(t_G(k)) for every polynomial p)' with 'generator poly(2^k·ℓ(k)), distinguishers circuits of size ℓ(k)² only — t_G(k) > ℓ(k)² allowed'. (iii) Compare 'uniform PPT + negligible gap 1/p(k)' (non-uniform variant: poly-size circuits, still negligible gap) with 'non-uniform circuit family of size ℓ(k)² + constant gap 1/6'. For the closing comparison: a polynomial-stretch generator feeding n^c coins needs n^{Ω(1)}-bit seeds, so enumeration costs 2^{n^{Ω(1)}}; an exponential-stretch derandomizer feeds n^c coins from O(log n)-bit seeds, so enumeration costs poly(n).

exercises.prompt: Let t(n) = n^c (c ≥ 1) be the time and randomness complexity of some algorithm in BPtime(t). For each stretch function below, compute (up to polynomial factors) the seed length k = ℓ^{-1}(t(n)) and the derandomization time T(n) = poly(2^{ℓ^{-1}(t(n))} · t(n)) promised by Proposition 3.2, and decide whether BPtime(t) ⊆ Dtime(poly(n)) follows: (i) ℓ(k) = k + 1; (ii) ℓ(k) = k²; (iii) ℓ(k) = 2^{√k}; (iv) ℓ(k) = 2^{k/2}. Then prove that no canonical derandomizer can have super-exponential stretch ℓ(k) = ω(2^k): exhibit the circuit, its size, and its distinguishing gap, and check it against Eq. (3.1). Conclude with a sentence on why 'stretch 2^{Ω(k)}' is the exact prize — the boundary below which derandomization is exponential and above which nothing exists.
exercises.hint: Solve ℓ(k) ≈ u for u = t(n): (i) k = u − 1, T = 2^{O(u)}; (ii) k = √u = n^{c/2}, T = 2^{O(n^{c/2})}; (iii) k = (log₂ u)² = c² log₂² n, T = poly(2^{c² log² n}) = n^{O(log n)} — quasi-polynomial, not polynomial; (iv) k = 2 log₂ u = 2c log₂ n, T = poly(2^{2c log n}·n^c) = poly(n). For the ceiling: let D_k accept an input iff it equals one of the 2^k strings G(s) — a lookup table of size O(2^k·ℓ(k)) (each of the 2^k entries costs O(ℓ(k)) gates); compute Pr[D_k(G(U_k)) = 1], Pr[D_k(U_ℓ(k)) = 1], the gap, and compare O(2^k·ℓ(k)) with ℓ(k)² when ℓ(k) = ω(2^k).

exercises.prompt: (a) Show that for any function G: {0,1}^k → {0,1}^{ℓ(k)} with ℓ(k) ≥ k + 1, the variation distance between G(U_k) and U_ℓ(k) is at least 1 − 2^{k−ℓ(k)}; evaluate this for exponential stretch and explain why the statistical distance does not contradict Definition 3.1 — where does the 'computational' part enter, and why is the derandomization application untouched by it? (b) Explain precisely why the uniform 'enumerate all seeds' distinguisher does not refute Definition 3.1, and why — in the opposite direction — no general-purpose PRG in the sense of Definition 2.1 can be secure against a distinguisher that receives the seed as auxiliary input, while (as the next lesson shows) a canonical derandomizer can be. Which resource asymmetry is responsible for both facts? (c) Give the structural reasons why the re-seeding / stretch-amplification techniques of Section 2.4 cannot be ported to the canonical-derandomizer regime, and explain why this failure is a feature: it forces exponential stretch to be built in one shot rather than by sequential composition.
exercises.hint: (a) Count supports: G(U_k) has at most 2^k atoms, each receiving total mass 1; U_ℓ(k) spreads mass 2^{−ℓ(k)} per point, so the overlap of the two distributions is at most 2^k·2^{−ℓ(k)}; TV = 1 − overlap. Then note that the tests witnessing this distance (e.g., range membership) have complexity ≈ 2^k·ℓ(k), far beyond the size-ℓ(k)² circuits of Eq. (3.1), and that derandomization only needs each C_x to behave the same under both distributions — the distance itself is irrelevant to correctness. (b) The enumerator runs in time 2^k·t_G(k) ≥ 2^k·ℓ(k) > ℓ(k)² (for ℓ(k) < 2^k; larger stretches are impossible): not a size-ℓ(k)² circuit. For Chapter 2: t_G(k) = poly(k), so a PPT distinguisher given the seed can simply evaluate G on it and compare with the suffix — seed-revealing security is impossible; but the size-ℓ(k)² circuits of Definition 3.1 cannot run the poly(2^k·ℓ(k))-time G. (c) Amplification reductions simulate the base generator inside the hybrids, costing 2^{Ω(k)} ≫ ℓ(k)² circuit resources, and re-seeding compounds polynomial stretch only — it cannot jump to the exponential ceiling.
